title: The Harmandir's day
hook: the Granth is carried in a palki to rest at night and returned at dawn

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ravidassia community, keeping Guru Ravidas at the center of a path now their own. Your line was their own path. Whose words did you use back to them? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

Amritsar, before first light. The water around the Harmandir Sahib is black and flat, and the gold looks almost gray. People are already waiting along the causeway, some barefoot on cold marble, some with small children asleep on their shoulders. Then a drum, and a conch, and a crowd begins to move. Shoulders press in, hands reach out to touch the poles of something being carried. A palki, a palanquin, is coming home. Inside it is a book, wrapped in cloth, and the people reaching for it call that book the Guru. This path has watched the night crossing once already. Today, the whole day around it.
screen: `AMRITSAR, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A DRUM, A CONCH, A CROWD.` → `A PALKI COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Begin before the light. In the Japji, Guru Nanak points to the ambrosial hours, the early dark before dawn, here in paraphrase: in those hours, dwell on the true Name and its greatness. The Harmandir's day starts there. The Granth is carried back from its night room, set on its high seat under a canopy, and opened. Sikhs call this the prakash, the light, when the Guru is brought out and opened for the day. Then a hymn is read from the opened page: the Guru's word for that morning. Now the long middle. All day, singers take turns in the sanctum, and the hymns of the Granth are sung on, set after set, while people file across the causeway, bow, listen for a moment, and move on. The doors stay open. The kitchen keeps feeding. The Guru is, in Sikh language, holding court. Then night. After the evening prayers, the Granth is closed, wrapped, and carried out again in the palki, to rest. Sikhs call this sukhasan, the seat of ease. Not storage. Rest. That's today's line: carried to rest. And here's the heart of it. Why would anyone carry a book to bed? Because Sikhs don't treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a book they own. They treat it as the living Guru, the one Guru Gobind Singh named before he died. A living Guru wakes, gives the word, keeps company, and rests. So the ritual isn't about the paper. It's about how you'd treat someone you revere if they lived in your house. Gurdwaras do a version of this too, in a quiet back room, and so do homes that keep the Granth. At the Harmandir it simply happens in front of the crowd.
screen: `THE AMBROSIAL HOURS BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRAKASH: THE GURU OPENED FOR THE DAY.` · `ALL DAY, THE HYMNS SUNG ON.` · `SUKHASAN: CARRIED TO REST.` · then, large: `A LIVING GURU WAKES AND RESTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the ceremony. Live video from the Harmandir is streamed online, and after the bell you can look for the palki there. For now, settle, and breathe. See the causeway in the dark, the palki on the shoulders of the crowd, the drum and the conch. Then see the evening, the same palki going the other way. Between those two crossings, a whole day of hymns. Breathe in at the dawn crossing. Breathe out at the night one. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The Harmandir's day. The Granth opened at dawn in the prakash, sung all day, and carried at night in the palki to rest, in sukhasan. Today's word.
Your line: carried to rest. Tonight, put one thing you treasure away with care, a book, a photo, an instrument, as if it deserved a proper rest. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: At the Harmandir Sahib the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in a palki before dawn for the prakash and carried back at night for sukhasan; gurdwaras and homes that keep the Granth follow the same pattern on a smaller scale.
